passage:
Gopika, you asked why I go quiet when people say "tell him from me". Your Vijay Mama will tell you.
When I was nineteen, my parents lived in one house but spoke only through me. At breakfast my father would clear his throat and say, "Tell your mother the electricity bill is not paid by magic." I carried it across the kitchen. My mother would say, "Tell him some of us work without being thanked." I carried that back.
Soon each of them began saying, "You understand me better than your mother," or, "You're the only sensible one, not like your father." I felt chosen and trapped at once. Whichever message I softened, one of them called me a traitor.
One evening I set down the tea and said, "From today, whatever you want to say, say it to each other." My legs were shaking.
It didn't fix them. But it gave me back my own place in that house.

qa.q: What did Vijay's father tell him to pass on at breakfast?
qa.a: His father said, "Tell your mother the electricity bill is not paid by magic."

qa.q: How did young Vijay feel when each parent called him the sensible one?
qa.a: He felt chosen and trapped at once, flattered but afraid of being called a traitor by whichever parent he disappointed.

qa.q: What choice inside the story gave young Vijay back his place?
qa.a: Setting down the tea and telling his parents to say things to each other, even with his legs shaking, stepped him out of the middle.

qa.q: How might Vijay's mother have felt when he refused to carry messages?
qa.a: She may have felt surprised and perhaps a little ashamed to see her son caught between them, and pushed to speak to his father directly.

grounding: An uncle recalls being used at nineteen as a go-between for his parents' hurtful messages, feeling divided and unsafe, and finally refusing to carry them.

The wedding hall was so loud with the band that Usha had to lean close to hear Akash, and she wished she hadn't.
"Kriti would've worn something brighter," he said of his ex, eyes on the stage. "She always knew how to dress for these things."
It was the fourth Kriti comment that month. Kriti cooked better. Kriti never got tired at parties. Each time Usha laughed it off, and each time she checked her reflection twice afterwards.
Now, in the crush near the food counter, a woman in a green saree said, "Arre, Akash! Where's Kriti these days?" Akash grinned. "Ask Usha, she's always thinking about her."
Usha felt her face burn. She wasn't thinking about Kriti. She was worried about never being enough.
Outside, by the parked scooters, she called her friend Mehak. "Can you pick me up? I'll explain on the way."

qa.q: How many Kriti comments had Akash made that month?
qa.a: It was the fourth Kriti comment that month.

qa.q: What was Usha truly worried about?
qa.a: She was worried about never being enough, not about Kriti, which shows how the comparisons had worn her down.

qa.q: Why was calling Mehak a wise step for Usha?
qa.a: Stepping out of the loud hall and calling a friend gave Usha support and space to think, instead of laughing off one more comparison.

qa.q: How does Akash seem to see his Kriti comments?
qa.a: He treats them as casual remarks and even jokes about them in public, seeming not to notice or care how much they unsettle Usha.

grounding: A young woman repeatedly compared to Akash's ex feels anxious and never good enough, and steps out of a wedding to call a friend for support.

passage:
Every Saturday, Vishal took the bus from his college in the town back to the village, and every Saturday, his father Santosh met him at the stop with a message.
"Tell your mother the house is still in my name. Tell her she can't keep the buffalo." Then, at his mother's house on the other side of the village, she'd say, "Tell your father I'm not scared of him."
Vishal carried the words back and forth like hot coals. He loved them both. He hated being the bridge between their fights. On the bus back each Sunday, his stomach churned. He never knew which parent would be angry with him for what the other had said.
One Saturday, at the bus stop, he said, "Papa, I won't carry messages anymore. If you want to tell Amma something, call her yourself, or ask the panchayat. I'll visit you both. As your son. Not as a postman."
Santosh stared at him, then looked away.

qa.q: What did Santosh tell Vishal to say about the house?
qa.a: Tell your mother the house is still in my name.

qa.q: How did Vishal feel carrying the messages?
qa.a: Vishal felt anxious and torn, his stomach churning, loving both parents but hating being the bridge in their fights.

qa.q: What boundary did Vishal set?
qa.a: He refused to carry messages anymore, suggested his father call directly or go to the panchayat, and said he'd visit both as their son.

qa.q: How might Santosh feel when Vishal refuses?
qa.a: Santosh may feel surprised and a little ashamed, which is why he stares and then looks away.

grounding: It shows a young adult used by separated parents to carry hurtful messages, feeling divided loyalty, and refusing to be the go-between.

subtype: Being compared or used as a go-between [Receiver]
passage:
In Stockholm, Nadia's parents had been separated for a year, and Nadia, home from university for the weekend, was helping her mother Ulla carry groceries up the stairs.
"When you see your father tomorrow," Ulla said, "tell him I know about the new girlfriend. And tell him the car payment was late again."
Nadia's shoulders tightened. It was always like this. Every visit, a message for one side and a message for the other. Her father did it too: "Ask your mother why she's spending so much."
She never felt safe in either apartment. Whatever she said, someone would be hurt, and it would feel like her fault.
Nadia put the bags down on the landing. "Mamma, I love you. But I'm not going to pass that on. If you need to talk to Pappa, please talk to him directly. I just want to be your daughter."
Ulla was quiet for a long moment. Then she said, "You're right. I'm sorry."

qa.q: What did Ulla ask Nadia to tell her father about the car payment?
qa.a: Tell him the car payment was late again.

qa.q: How did Nadia feel being asked to pass messages?
qa.a: Nadia felt anxious and never safe in either apartment, afraid that whatever she said would hurt someone and feel like her fault.

qa.q: What did Nadia do to protect herself?
qa.a: She lovingly refused to pass the message on and asked her mother to talk to her father directly.

qa.q: How did Ulla respond to Nadia's words?
qa.a: Ulla was quiet, then admitted Nadia was right and apologised.

grounding: It shows a young adult used by separated parents to carry hurtful messages, feeling divided and unsafe, and asking them to speak directly.

passage: In the hostel visitors' room, Chandrika sat with her phone on speaker while her roommate Charu pretended to read. "Tell your father," her mother said, "that if he can afford a new car, he can afford your fees on time. Tell him exactly that." Chandrika's stomach dropped. Last week her father had asked her to "mention" to her mother that she'd always been bad with money. Every Sunday call now came with a message to carry. "Amma, can you tell him yourself?" "Why should I talk to that man? You're his daughter." After the call, Chandrika pressed her palms into her eyes. "If I pass it on, Papa gets angry at me. If I don't, Amma says I've taken his side." Charu put the book down. "You're not their post office. The student counsellor sees people for exactly this. Want me to come with you tomorrow?" Chandrika nodded, slowly.

qa.q: What did Chandrika's mother want her to tell her father?
qa.a: That if he can afford a new car, he can afford her fees on time.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling after the call?
qa.a: Chandrika felt anxious and torn between her parents: passing it on makes Papa angry, and refusing makes Amma say she's taken his side.

qa.q: What could help Chandrika step out of the go-between role?
qa.a: She could tell each parent kindly that she won't carry messages, and take up Charu's offer to see the student counsellor for support.

qa.q: How does Charu see the situation?
qa.a: Charu sees Chandrika being used as a post office between her parents and offers practical support by going to the counsellor together.

grounding: Shows a young adult used by parents to carry hurtful messages to each other, left anxious and torn in loyalty.
